title: "Properties of estimators"

An estimate is one realized number. An **estimator** is the rule that would produce an estimate from every possible sample, and its [**sampling distribution**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat200/Lesson04) describes the estimates that rule would produce across repeated samples.

How can we see this distinction rather than simply state it? We will repeatedly resample the observed speakers and apply the same rule to every resample. The resulting values make a bootstrap approximation to the estimator's sampling distribution visible, which lets us introduce the properties studied on the next pages. The later [confidence-interval page](confidence-intervals.qmd) applies the same repeated-sampling logic to two random endpoints.

## A nonparametric bootstrap from the observed cohort

We use the vowel measurements of Hillenbrand et al. ([1995](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872)), obtained through [`phonTools::h95`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=phonTools). The package uses the BSD-2-Clause license, which does not independently establish the reuse terms for the historical observations. The study recorded 45 adult men, 48 adult women, 27 boys, and 19 girls producing the same 12 /hVd/ vowels. One row is one vowel token nested within a speaker.

The prepared table contains complete duration measurements. Its F2 and F3 columns include package-supplied imputations, but those columns play no role here. We focus on the 48 adult women producing /I/ in *hid*. A [nonparametric bootstrap](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1176344552) samples these observed speaker rows with replacement. It is useful for studying estimator behavior conditional on the cohort, but it does not reconstruct recruitment from all American English speakers.

Sampling with replacement means that the empirical distribution assigns probability $1/n$ to each observed speaker. A bootstrap sample may thus contain one speaker several times and omit another. This device approximates repeated sampling from the empirical distribution; it is not a claim that the original investigators recruited speakers with replacement.

```{r}
#| label: load-hillenbrand-estimators
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv(
  "data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
women_hid <- subset(vowels, speaker_type == "woman" & vowel == "I")
x <- women_hid$duration_ms
target_mean <- mean(x)
target_sd <- sqrt(mean((x - target_mean)^2))

stopifnot(nrow(women_hid) == 48L, !anyDuplicated(women_hid$speaker_id))

data.frame(
  speakers = length(x),
  empirical_mean_ms = target_mean,
  empirical_median_ms = median(x),
  empirical_sd_ms = target_sd,
  minimum_ms = min(x),
  maximum_ms = max(x)
)
```

## Estimators are random variables

For a sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the sample-mean estimator is

$$
T(\mathbf X)=\overline X=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nX_i.
$$

Before sampling, $T(\mathbf X)$ is a random variable. After observing one sample $\mathbf x$, $T(\mathbf x)$ is an estimate. A useful sampling distribution is described by its expectation and variance:

The [random-variable chapter](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd) explains why a function of random observations is itself random. [Expectation](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd) averages its possible values using their probabilities, while [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) averages squared deviations from that expectation.

$$
\mathbb{E}[T(\mathbf X)]
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[T(\mathbf X)].
$$

The three roles can be kept separate as follows:

| Role | Symbol here | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| estimator | $T(\mathbf X)$ | a rule applied to a random sample |
| estimate | $T(\mathbf x)$ | the number produced from the observed sample |
| target | $\theta$ | the fixed quantity the rule is intended to estimate |

The following simulation uses the observed adult-women group size and a fixed seed. The resampling unit is a speaker row.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-hillenbrand-estimator
set.seed(20261018)
replicates <- 20000L
sample_size <- nrow(women_hid)
sample_means <- replicate(
  replicates,
  mean(sample(x, size = sample_size, replace = TRUE))
)

sampling_center <- mean(sample_means)
sampling_sd <- sd(sample_means)

stopifnot(abs(sampling_center - target_mean) < 0.25)

data.frame(
  replicates = replicates,
  sample_size = sample_size,
  target_mean_ms = target_mean,
  mean_of_estimates_ms = sampling_center,
  sampling_sd_ms = sampling_sd
)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-estimator
#| fig-cap: "Empirical sampling distribution of the mean /I/ duration from speaker-row resamples. The line marks the empirical cohort mean."
ggplot(data.frame(mean_ms = sample_means), aes(mean_ms)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 42,
                 fill = "grey75", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = target_mean, color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Mean /I/ duration in a speaker resample (ms)", y = "Simulation density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The estimates vary even though the empirical target remains fixed at `r sprintf("%.3f", target_mean)` ms. This distinction between response variation and estimator variation is the foundation for standard errors, bias, and confidence intervals.

## Recap and forward link

1. An estimator is a random variable because it is a function of random observations.
2. An estimate is one realized value of that estimator.
3. The bootstrap distribution approximates repeated empirical-distribution sampling, conditional on this cohort.
4. Resampling speakers preserves the unit represented by each row in this subset.

The [standard-error page](standard-errors.qmd#deriving-the-standard-error-of-a-mean) relates the spread of this sampling distribution to sample size.

## Check your understanding

1. Which object changes across the bootstrap samples, and which target remains fixed?
2. What is the resampling unit?
3. Why would resampling all twelve vowel rows independently break the speaker structure?
4. What population claim does this nonparametric bootstrap not license?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The resampled speaker rows, and thus the estimated means, change across draws; the empirical cohort mean remains fixed. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The resampling unit is one adult-woman speaker row for /I/ in *hid*. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The twelve vowel measurements from one speaker are dependent. Row-wise resampling would separate measurements that belong to the same speaker. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. This nonparametric bootstrap does not license a claim about all American English speakers or reproduce the study's recruitment process. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
